21323-what-the-church-means-to-me-a-fran:
Wilfred T. Grenfell, the doctor and missionary famous for his medical mission in Labrador, published this frank confession in 1911. The church, he says, means all who are forwarding God's kingdom on earth, consciously or not. Any body that claims the title for itself alone, he calls ridiculous.

Through the church, Grenfell writes, came his spiritual sight, strength in weakness, comfort in trial, and help in need. He argues that how people organise worship gives no one a right to exclude others doing Christ's work another way. It is a short, warm statement from a practical Christian who spent his life running hospitals, ships, and schools in the North.
35119-trenching-at-gallipoli-the-persona:
Trenching at Gallipoli, a war memoir by John Gallishaw, was published in New York in 1916. Gallishaw served as a Newfoundlander with the Dardanelles Expedition. His subtitle calls the book a personal narrative of that failed campaign. Photographs from the front fill the book.

Nine chapters trace his path from enlistment to home. They cover the trip out, the landing, trench life, and dugouts. Later chapters deal with waiting, patrols in no mans land, and being wounded. The last part follows the trip home. The book stands as a first hand record of the Gallipoli campaign from a colonial soldier in the ranks.
41335-automatic-pistol-shooting-together:
Automatic Pistol Shooting, together with information on handling the duelling pistol and revolver, is a marksmanship manual by Walter Winans. Putnam's Sons published it in New York and London in 1915. Winans's honours fill his title page: Olympic champion for double-rifle shooting in 1908 and gold medallist at Stockholm in 1912. He was also revolver champion of the National Rifle Association of Great Britain for five years.

The chapters begin with the automatic pistol itself, then selecting a pistol, and cleaning and care. A passage preserved in the copy gives his recommendations from personal experience. Two makes, he says, he can recommend. One is the Colt forty-five, which the United States Government adopted for army and navy purposes. He praises its grip, set at the proper angle for shooting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-gabrie:
Johann Gabriel Seidl, Austrian poet and author of the present national hymn's text, was born at Vienna in 1804 and died there in 1875. Of Swiss stock, son of an able lawyer and a capable housewife, he passed the gymnasium with distinction and entered university at fifteen for philosophy.

His father's early death forced Seidl to tutor himself and his mother, so he swapped law for teaching, qualified in 1827, and taught at Cilli's state gymnasium from 1829. False death notices praising him drew official notice. After eleven happy years he returned to Vienna as keeper of the imperial medal cabinet, later book censor to 1848, Academy member, and imperial treasurer.
